newsitem.title: USA: U.S Fed watchers revisit growth/inflation relation.
newsitem.headline: U.S Fed watchers revisit growth/inflation relation.

text.p: Fed watchers are revisiting the relationship between growth and inflation as a slew of Wall Street firms now expect the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) to raise the federal funds rate on March 25.

"If the Federal Reserve does not raise rates next week, this would indicate they truly believe there has been a structural change in the U.S. economy," said Ken Bercuson, chief economist at SBC Warburg who has been predicting a March 25-point hike in the 5.25-percent funds rate since early this year, and another at the May 20 FOMC meeting.

"The only ground for waiting is to think the economy has changed so much that, even with this pace of consumer spending, inflation is not a problem. It would mean they are willing to see whether that change has indeed taken place, be no longer preemptive, and willing to tighten only when inflation moves up," Bercuson also said.
This view now prevails on Wall Street, where most analysts expect an imminent rate hike, the first such in two years.
Three Reuters polls taken between between late February and March 20 showed the number of Fed watchers at the 37 U.S. primary dealers expecting a tightening next week stood at:
-- 7 on February 27, following Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony where he warned of "the distribution of inflation risks skewed to the upside."
-- 16 on March 11, following the February employment, with payrolls up 339,000 and the jobless rate at 5.3 percent.

-- 29 on March 20, following the February Consumer Price Index, up 3.0 percent year-over-year. Five of these firms changed their forecasts around Thursday noon, following Greenspan's testimony before the Joint Economic Committee.
They are Bear, Stearns and Co, Citicorp Securities, Chase Securities, Merrill Lynch, and Prudential Securities.
Peter Kretzmer, senior economist at NationsBanc Capital Markets, said his firm changed its forecast after the CPI.
Earlier, NationsBanc did not forecast a rate hike on March 25 nor at the following FOMC meeting on May 20.

"Growth is clearly above trend, and Greenspan interprets it to mean that perhaps signs of the inflation process may be beginning," said Kretzmer, who described the change in his firm's forecast "a very close call."
The year-over-year core CPI, ex-food and ex-energy, has stopped declining in recent months but is holding at a historically low reading of 2.5 percent.
Kretzmer added Greenspan will decide "that one tightening would benefit the Fed's credibility further."
PNC Bank chief economist Stuart Hoffman, who thinks the Fed may wait until May to raise rates, admitted he now has doubts about that forecast.

"The strength in the economy is no doubt related to the monetary policy of six to nine months ago," Hoffman said, referring to the Fed's absence of move last fall despite signs the economy was packing momentum in 1996.
"But I don't believe there is a lot of inflation baked in the cake over what the Fed did last year," Hoffman added.
Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities, changed his forecast from no move to a March tightening "because of the payrolls and the February retail sales."

"Policy depends of what is happening with the strength of the economy," Moran explained. "When we saw the retail and employment reports, this meant growth will remain brisk, probably in excess of 3.0 percent in the first quarter."

Moran said Greenspan's emphasis on preemptive policy means "the growth rate is telling us policy needs to be tighter. If the Fed moves now, it could still be considered preemptive. Waiting longer would be waiting too long."
-- "Maybe/5.50," indicates the firm expected one single 25-bps move in March or May.
-- (*) indicates the firm changed its forecast or altered it to clarify the date:
